# Intake Noise as an Early Warning for Cartridge-Filter Loading

## Operational question

Morrow Shoal Desalination Works is a 52 ML/day seawater reverse-osmosis plant whose cartridge filters sometimes load rapidly after rough weather. Operators currently respond to intake turbidity, but suspended shell fragments and fibrous seaweed do not always produce a large turbidity increase. This analysis examines whether noise recorded by an intake hydrophone could provide an earlier warning.

The proposed measure is the **Nereid sound index**, a score from 0 to 100 based on acoustic energy between 1 and 8 kHz. The plant’s engineering team suggested that harder particles and tangled debris striking the intake screen would increase the score before that material reached the cartridge filters. The practical aim was to identify periods when operators should reduce plant flow or inspect the filters.

## Data

The dataset covers 142 operating days from 3 February to 24 June 2025. Readings were aligned into ten-minute intervals from four sources:

- Nereid sound index at the offshore intake;
- conventional intake turbidity in NTU;
- cartridge-filter differential pressure in bar;
- operating records, including flow, tide, seawater temperature, filter changes and shutdowns.

There were 20,448 possible ten-minute intervals. A total of 1,596 intervals were removed because the hydrophone was offline, mainly during two storms, and 432 were removed during shutdowns or the first hour after a filter change. This left 18,420 intervals for analysis. Missing hydrophone readings were not filled because interpolation would conceal sudden noise peaks.

A filter-loading outcome was defined as a differential-pressure increase of at least 0.35 bar during the following six hours. There were 504 positive intervals under this definition. These intervals corresponded to 21 recorded pressure-rise incidents, because several consecutive observations could point to the same later incident.

The analysis used the measured differential pressure rather than a flow-normalized pressure. Plant flow was usually between 47 and 52 ML/day, although it fell below 45 ML/day on 18 days.

## Method

First, average sound index values were compared between intervals followed by a pressure rise and all other intervals. A two-sample t-test was used to judge whether the difference was statistically significant. A linear regression was then fitted with six-hour pressure change as the outcome and sound index, seawater temperature and tidal stage as predictors.

For alarm performance, sound-index thresholds from 40 to 80 were tested in steps of two points. A threshold of 68 gave the highest F1 score and was selected as the proposed alarm level. The same dataset was used both to select and report this threshold because a separate test period was not available.

Performance was compared with the plant’s existing turbidity alarm, which activates above 1.6 NTU. Each ten-minute interval was classified as a true positive, false positive, false negative or true negative. No adjustment was made for neighboring intervals belonging to the same event.

## Results

The mean sound index was 71.4 before a defined pressure rise, compared with 42.8 during other intervals. The difference was statistically significant at p < 0.001. The fitted regression suggested that each ten-point increase in sound index was associated with a 0.061 bar greater differential-pressure increase over the next six hours. Temperature and tide had smaller coefficients, and the model had an R² of 0.27.

Alarm results were as follows:

| Alarm rule | True positive | False positive | False negative | True negative | Sensitivity | Precision |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sound index ≥68 | 391 | 271 | 113 | 17,645 | 77.6% | 59.1% |
| Turbidity >1.6 NTU | 244 | 186 | 260 | 17,730 | 48.4% | 56.7% |

The sound alarm therefore identified about three-quarters of positive intervals, compared with roughly half for turbidity. Its precision was only slightly higher, and it generated 85 more false-positive intervals. However, these false positives were concentrated into 14 clusters rather than 271 separate operating episodes. If one inspection were made per cluster, the workload would be more manageable than the interval count suggests.

Nine of the 14 false-positive clusters occurred while intake pumps were running above 95% of their rated load. This may indicate that pump or pipe noise was being recorded as debris noise. It could also mean that high flow brought in material that did not produce a pressure increase large enough to meet the 0.35 bar outcome threshold. The current data do not distinguish these explanations.

Manual intake samples were available for 12 days. On seven days when the sound index exceeded 68, operators recorded shell grit or fibrous material in at least one sample. Material was recorded on only one of the five sampled days without an acoustic alarm. The sample records support the proposed mechanism, although sampling was irregular and operators were more likely to collect material after unusual plant readings.

## Operational and financial interpretation

Plant logs recorded 15 unplanned cartridge-filter changes during the study period. Eleven occurred during or after clusters in which the sound index exceeded 68. Assuming this proportion continues, an acoustic alarm might allow approximately nine changes per year to be scheduled earlier or avoided by temporarily reducing flow.

The plant estimates that an unplanned filter change costs $4,200 in cartridges, labor and lost production. Nine avoided changes would therefore save $37,800 annually. A permanent hydrophone, signal processor and control-room display are estimated to cost $38,000, with annual maintenance of $6,000. On these assumptions, simple payback would be about 1.2 years after maintenance costs are deducted. This calculation does not include revenue lost during precautionary flow reductions or the labor cost of responding to false alarms.

A high sound index did not guarantee rapid filter loading. Almost two-fifths of alarm intervals were false positives, and the regression explained only 27% of pressure-change variation. The hydrophone was also unavailable during some of the roughest weather, so its performance in the conditions of greatest interest is uncertain. Seasonal changes after June were not observed.

## Recommendation

Morrow Shoal should run the sound alarm in advisory mode for three additional months rather than connecting it directly to plant controls. Operators should record whether each alarm coincides with debris, pump-speed changes or actual filter loading. Differential pressure should also be normalized for flow, and alarm performance should be assessed by independent incidents rather than ten-minute intervals.

For the trial, a score of 68 is a reasonable starting point. The alarm appears to detect loading conditions that turbidity misses, but automatic flow reduction would be premature until the pump-noise effect and false-alarm cost are better understood.
planted_strengths: The write-up clearly defines the operational question, data sources, exclusions, outcome, alarm threshold and comparison baseline.
It reports a complete confusion matrix and translates interval-level results into operational alarm clusters, making the findings more useful to plant staff.
It acknowledges several practical limitations and recommends an advisory pilot rather than immediate automated control.
planted_weaknesses: The analysis treats overlapping ten-minute intervals as independent even though 504 positive intervals arise from only 21 incidents, producing pseudoreplication and an overstated p-value and effective sample size.
The alarm threshold is optimized and evaluated on the same dataset, with no holdout period or cross-validation, so reported performance is likely optimistic.
Differential pressure is not normalized for flow, while pump loading can affect both hydrophone noise and filter pressure; this major confound undermines the claimed predictive relationship.
Hydrophone observations are disproportionately missing during storms, so missingness is not random and may bias results for the most important operating conditions.

The financial estimate assumes that an early alarm would prevent nine filter changes, although the observational data show only association and do not establish that operator intervention would avoid those changes.
quality_rationale: The artefact has credible operational framing, readable tables, transparent exclusions and a cautious pilot recommendation. However, its central statistical analysis is weak: it inflates the sample through overlapping observations, selects and tests the threshold on the same data, does not control adequately for flow and pump noise, and converts an observational association into speculative savings. These substantive flaws make the headline performance and payback estimates unreliable despite the useful descriptive work.
title: Intake Noise as an Early Warning for Cartridge-Filter Loading
topic: Analysis of whether underwater intake noise can predict rapid cartridge-filter loading at a fictional seawater reverse-osmosis plant.
